title: Arjuna's Question and Stories Inside the Story
bigQuestion: What should you do when your duty feels too hard?

story.title: Following Death
story.kicker: A bride walks behind Death himself and will not stop asking.
paragraphs: Deep in a forest, a young woman named Savitri sits under a tree. Her husband, Satyavan, rests his head in her lap. He has been cutting wood all morning. Now he is very still.
A tall figure in dark red appears among the trees. He carries a noose. It is Yama, the lord of death. He has come for Satyavan's life, and he turns to leave.
Savitri stands up and follows him. Yama tells her to go home. She keeps walking. She speaks to him calmly and wisely about goodness and friendship. Yama is surprised.
Yama is pleased by her words. He offers her a wish, anything except her husband's life. She asks for something else. He offers another wish. She keeps following and keeps speaking.
At last, Savitri asks for a wish that Yama cannot grant unless Satyavan lives. Yama smiles and gives her husband back. This story is one of many stories told inside the Mahabharata.
story.think: Savitri did not fight Death. How did she win?

lessons.title: The Song of the Lord
lessons.mainIdea: The Bhagavad Gita is an 18-chapter teaching inside the Mahabharata.
reading: The *Bhagavad Gita* means "the song of the Lord." It is found in the sixth book of the Mahabharata, the Bhishma Parva. It has 18 chapters and 700 verses.
The whole Gita is a conversation. It takes place on the battlefield of Kurukshetra, just before the war begins. Arjuna asks questions, and Krishna answers them.
Many Hindus treasure the Gita above almost any other text. It has been translated into English and hundreds of other languages. Many families keep a copy at their home shrine.

words.d: "the song of the Lord"; Krishna's teaching to Arjuna in the Mahabharata
a talk between two or more people

lessons.title: Arjuna Puts Down His Bow
lessons.mainIdea: Arjuna does not want to fight his own relatives and teachers.
reading: Arjuna rides into the middle of the battlefield. He looks at the other army. He sees his uncles, his cousins, his friends and his beloved teacher, Drona.
Arjuna's body shakes. His mouth goes dry. He tells Krishna he does not want a kingdom if it means killing his own family. He sets down his bow and sits in the chariot.
The first chapter of the Gita is sometimes called "Arjuna's sorrow." Many readers see Arjuna's pain as very human. Anyone can feel stuck when every choice seems wrong.

words.d: the Pandava archer whom Krishna teaches in the Gita
deep sadness

lessons.title: Krishna the Charioteer
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna, Arjuna's charioteer, becomes his teacher, and many Hindus honor him as God.
reading: In the Mahabharata, Krishna is Arjuna's friend and cousin. He agrees not to fight in the war. Instead, he drives Arjuna's chariot. A charioteer steers the horses.
When Arjuna sits down in despair, Krishna becomes his teacher. Later in the Gita, Krishna says he is God. Many Hindus honor Krishna as an avatar of Vishnu, or as God himself.
Many Hindu pictures show this scene. Krishna holds the reins of white horses and turns to speak. Arjuna listens with his hands folded. Families often hang this picture at home.

words.d: the person who drives a chariot
a form in which, Hindus believe, a deity comes into the world

lessons.title: Do Your Duty, Not for the Reward
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna teaches Arjuna to do his duty without being greedy for the reward.
reading: One of the most famous verses in the Gita is 2.47. In it, Krishna says Arjuna has a right to his work, but not to its results. He should act without clinging to the reward.
Think of a student who studies hard because learning matters, not only for a prize. Many Hindus read this verse as advice to do good work and let go of worry about results.
Krishna calls this *karma yoga*, the path of action. Karma means action. In this path, a person does their duty well and offers the results to God, as many Hindus understand it.

words.d: action; also the idea that actions bring results
in the Gita, the path of doing your duty without clinging to the reward

lessons.title: The Self That Does Not Die
lessons.mainIdea: Krishna teaches that the true self, the atman, is never born and never dies.
reading: Krishna tells Arjuna not to grieve. He teaches that the true self, the *atman*, is not the body. The body is born and dies, but, the Gita says, the atman does not.
The Gita compares this to changing clothes. As a person throws away worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves one body and takes on another (Gita 2.22).
This idea of being born again and again is called *samsara*. Many Hindus believe in samsara. Other religions have different beliefs about what happens after death.

words.d: the true self inside each being
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth

check.why: Gita 2.22 compares bodies to clothes that are changed.

lessons.title: Many Ways to Read the Gita
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus and others read the Gita in many different ways.
reading: The Gita describes several paths. One is the path of action. One is the path of knowledge. One is *bhakti*, the path of loving devotion to God. Many Hindus say the Gita honors all three.
Readers also disagree about the battle. Some read it as a real war and a lesson about duty. Mahatma Gandhi read the battle as a picture of the struggle between good and bad inside each person.
Great Hindu teachers wrote commentaries on the Gita, explaining it in different ways. Today, families, students and leaders around the world still read it and argue about its meaning.

words.d: loving devotion to God

look.title: Two Readers, One Battle

lessons.title: Savitri and Satyavan
lessons.mainIdea: Savitri chooses Satyavan as her husband, even though she knows he will die soon.
reading: During the Pandavas' forest exile, a sage tells them many stories. One is about Princess *Savitri*. She chooses a young man named Satyavan to marry. He lives in the forest with his blind father.
A sage warns her that Satyavan will die in exactly one year. Savitri says she has chosen and will not change her mind. She marries him and lives simply in the forest.
As the day draws near, Savitri fasts and prays. On the last day, she goes with Satyavan into the woods. This is where Yama, the lord of death, comes for him.

words.d: the princess in the Mahabharata who wins her husband back from Death
to go without food for a time, often for a religious reason

look.title: A Brave Choice

lessons.title: Savitri Wins
lessons.mainIdea: With patience and wise words, Savitri wins Satyavan back from Yama.
reading: When Yama takes Satyavan's life, Savitri follows him. She speaks wisely about goodness and friendship. Yama is pleased and grants her wishes, but never her husband's life.
She asks for her father-in-law's sight and kingdom to be restored. Then she asks to have many children with Satyavan. Yama agrees without thinking. But that wish needs Satyavan alive!
Yama keeps his word and returns Satyavan's life. Many Hindu women honor Savitri with a yearly fast and prayers for their families. The story is in the Vana Parva.

words.d: the lord of death in Hindu stories
staying calm and steady while you wait or work

look.title: The Last Wish

lessons.title: Nala and Damayanti
lessons.mainIdea: Nala and Damayanti lose everything through dice, and their love and courage bring them back together.
reading: Another forest story is about King *Nala* and Queen Damayanti. Nala loses his kingdom to his brother in a game of dice, much like Yudhishthira. Both kings lose everything.
Nala and Damayanti are separated in the forest. Damayanti searches bravely for her husband. Nala, changed in form, works as a charioteer for another king.
In the end, Damayanti finds a clever way to bring Nala back. He wins back his kingdom. The story is told to Yudhishthira to give him hope during his own exile.

words.d: a king in a Mahabharata story who loses his kingdom at dice and wins it back
the feeling that good things can still happen

lessons.title: "What Is Here Is Everywhere"
lessons.mainIdea: The Mahabharata claims to contain everything, and many readers find their own lives in it.
reading: The Mahabharata makes a bold claim about itself. It says that what is found in it may be found elsewhere, but what is not found in it is found nowhere.
The epic holds family quarrels, friendship, love, war, grief, and questions about right and wrong. Many readers say they recognize their own lives in its stories.
The Mahabharata has been retold as TV shows, plays, novels and comics. In 1985, the director Peter Brook staged a famous version that ran for about nine hours. People keep finding new meanings in it.

words.d: a statement that something is true
